items.title: 26.3 Identification of the Type of a Polymer, Repeat Unit and Monomers from a Polymer Section

source_refs.note: Topic 26.3 as printed (PDF 152-154): the steps, Table 26.1 and the first Quick Check 26.2 (questions only, sections written as formulas). The printed schemes are the existing figures.

blocks.text: To identify a polymer from a skeletal or structural formula, you must look for the repeating linkage and the monomer units. At this level, only two classes of polymers are under discussion
Follow the given steps to identify the type of the polymer by considering the example of poly(ethene)

items: The first thing to check is what atoms make up the main horizontal chain of the polymer, i.e to identify the backbone.
If the main chain consists only of carbon atoms (-C-C-C-C-), it is an addition polymer. These are formed from alkenes.
If the main chain contains oxygen (O) or nitrogen (N) atoms with carbon, it is a condensation polymer (like polyesters or polyamides).

blocks.text: Now, identify the functional linkage. There are again two possibilities:

items: If a carbonyl group (C=O) is directly attached next to an oxygen (O). Such polymers are classified as polyesters. For example, PET has an ester linkage in the given section of its structure.

blocks.alt: Section of PET in brackets with subscript n: -C(=O)-benzene ring-C(=O)-O-CH2-CH2-O-. A small arrow points at the C=O of the ester linkage.
blocks.caption: PET section showing its ester linkage (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 152).

blocks.text: If there is a carbonyl group (C=O) directly next to a nitrogen (N) with a hydrogen (H) attached, it presents an amide or peptide linkage. The polymer is, therefore, classified as a polyamide (e.g., Nylon 6,6 or Kevlar).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book labels the first possibility “i.” (C=O next to O, an ester link) but prints this second possibility (C=O next to N–H, an amide link) without a label; it is possibility ii.

blocks.alt: Section of Kevlar: -N(H)-C(=O)-ring-C(=O)-N(H)-ring-N(H)-C(=O)-ring-C(=O)-N(H)-, with each C=O drawn upward and each N-H downward, showing the amide links between benzene rings.
blocks.caption: Kevlar section showing its amide linkages (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 152).

rows: Only C-C bonds in the chain

blocks.text: 2. Determining the Repeat Unit: To find the original monomers, one must first identify the smallest section that repeats itself in the section of the polymer.

items: To find the repeating pattern, look for where the sequence starts to duplicate itself. Locate such duplicating sections in the backbone.
Place brackets around one of these recurring sections and add the subscript n. This section within the brackets is the repeat unit of the polymer.
For addition polymers, change the C-C single bond in the repeat unit back into a C=C double bond to find the monomer.

blocks.alt: Part of addition polymer: a displayed chain of seven carbons with a benzene ring on every second carbon and H on the rest. An arrow leads to the repeat unit, [-CH(C6H5)-CH2-]n drawn in brackets, and another arrow to the monomer, H2C=CH(C6H5) (phenylethene).
blocks.caption: Identification of repeat unit and monomers (addition) (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 153).

items: For Condensation polymers: Add water back in. Break the ester or amide bond. Add -OH to the C=O side and -H to the O or N side as given below.

blocks.alt: Laid out as printed: part of condensation polymer (Kevlar), -NH-CO-ring-CO-NH-ring-NH-CO-ring-CO-NH-, at the left; an arrow right to the repeat unit [-NH-ring-NH-CO-ring-CO-]n; an arrow down from the repeat unit to the monomers H2N-ring-NH2 and HOOC-ring-COOH, or ClOC-ring-COCl.
blocks.caption: Identification of repeat unit and monomers (condensation) (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 153, which is captioned '(addition)').

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book captions the Kevlar scheme 'Identification of repeat unit and monomers (addition)'; Kevlar is a condensation polymer (amide links), so the figure is captioned (condensation).
a) Identify the type of polymerisation and monomers forming the following polymer sections.

blocks.explanation: The chain contains N, and each C=O is joined directly to an N–H, so this is a condensation polymer (a polyamide). The repeat unit is –CH₂–NH–CO–; the monomer is aminoethanoic acid (glycine), H₂N–CH₂–COOH.

blocks.alt: Displayed polymer section: -CH2-NH-CO-CH2-NH-CO-CH2-NH-CO-CH2-, with the N-H and C=O groups drawn alternately up and down.
blocks.caption: Quick Check 26.2 a i) polymer section (original drawing after the structure printed in the textbook on PDF page 154).

blocks.explanation: The chain contains only carbon atoms, so this is an addition polymer. The repeat unit is –CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)–; the monomer is phenylethene (styrene), CH₂=CH–C₆H₅.

blocks.alt: Skeletal polymer section: a zigzag carbon chain with a benzene ring on every second carbon, four rings shown, with dotted ends.
blocks.caption: Quick Check 26.2 a ii) polymer section (original drawing after the structure printed in the textbook on PDF page 154).

blocks.explanation: Addition polymer; the repeat unit is –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–; the monomer is propene, CH₂=CH–CH₃.

blocks.alt: Polymer section: -CH2CH(CH3)-CH2CH(CH3)-CH2CH(CH3)-, with a CH3 drawn above each CH, labelled Polypropylene.
blocks.caption: Quick Check 26.2 a iii) polymer section (original drawing after the structure printed in the textbook on PDF page 154).
